content:
# XAMPP Localhost Returns Object Not Found After Installing Laravel

Encountering an "Object not found!" or "The requested URL was not found on this server" error immediately after integrating a new framework into your existing stack is a classic symptom of Apache's `mod_rewrite` engine failing to parse the `.htaccess` configuration. This specific scenario often occurs when moving from a bare-bones XAMPP environment to a full Laravel installation. The core issue usually stems from a conflict between how your original virtual hosts were configured and the strict requirements Laravel imposes on its root directory permissions and file existence.

In many cases, users successfully deploy Laravel behind a custom domain name (like `laravel.dev`) but lose access to their default document root at `localhost`. This happens because Apache stops processing directives if it cannot locate the public directory specified in the VirtualHost block or if it hits a permission error before reaching the `.htaccess` file.

## The Root Cause: Missing Public Directory

The most common culprit is that the Laravel application structure has been placed directly into your `htdocs` folder without ensuring the existence of the `public` subdirectory, or the permissions on that directory are incorrect.

Laravel requires all web-accessible files to reside in a `public` folder within the project root. If you installed the framework directly into `/opt/lampp/htdocs` (on Windows) or `/Applications/MAMP/htdocs` (on macOS), Apache might be looking for an index file in the wrong place, triggering a 403 Forbidden or 404 Not Found response.

To resolve this, ensure your project structure looks like this:

```text
/opt/lampp/htdocs/
âââ laravel-project/
    âââ public/          # Must contain index.php and .htaccess
    âââ app/
    âââ resources/
    âââ vendor/
```

If you installed Laravel directly into the `htdocs` root, move the entire contents of your project into a subfolder named `public`. Then, create a new VirtualHost entry in your Apache configuration that points specifically to this directory.

## Configuring Virtual Hosts Correctly

When troubleshooting "Object not found" errors on localhost after installing Laravel, you must verify that your Apache configuration allows the request to reach the `.htaccess` file inside the `public` folder.

Edit your Apache virtual host configuration file (typically located at `/opt/lampp/etc/extra/httpd-vhosts.conf` or via XAMPP's "Apache Config" button in the control panel). You need a block that explicitly points to the `public` directory:

```apache
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName laravel.dev
    DocumentRoot "/opt/lampp/htdocs/laravel-project/public"
    
    <Directory "/opt/lampp/hosts/laravel-project/public">
        AllowOverride All
        Require all granted
    </Directory>
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName localhost
    DocumentRoot "/opt/lampp/htdocs/laravel-project/public"
    
    <Directory "/opt/lampp/hosts/laravel-project/public">
        AllowOverride All
        Require all granted
    </Directory>
</VirtualHost>
```

Notice the `DocumentRoot` directive; it must point to the folder containing `index.php`, not the project root itself. The `<Directory>` block ensures that Apache processes the `.htaccess` rules, which are crucial for routing requests to Laravel's front controller (`public/index.php`) rather than treating them as static file requests.

## Hosts File and DNS Resolution

You mentioned editing the `hosts` file to map `127.0.0.1` to `laravel.dev`. While this is a valid technique for testing, it can sometimes cause confusion if you are trying to access the site via `localhost` without a corresponding VirtualHost entry for that specific hostname.

If you undo the hosts file changes but still cannot access `localhost`, check whether your default XAMPP configuration has been overwritten. Sometimes, installing Laravel leads to a situation where the default `htdocs` index is missing or corrupted.

Ensure your `httpd.conf` or `extra/httpd-vhosts.conf` includes a default VirtualHost block for `localhost` that points to a valid directory (often a simple "Welcome to XAMPP" folder or a dedicated test project). If no default host exists, Apache may serve a 403 error when you request the root URL.

## Permission Checks and Security

Finally, verify file permissions. Laravel's documentation recommends setting the public directory permissions to `755`. On macOS or Linux-based XAMPP installations, incorrect permissions can prevent Apache from reading the `.htaccess` file or executing PHP scripts.

Run the following command in your terminal (if applicable):

```bash
chmod -R 755 /opt/lampp/htdocs/laravel-project/public
chown -R www-data:www-data /opt/lampp/htdocs/laravel-project/public
```

If you are on Windows, ensure that the `public` folder properties allow "Read & Execute" for everyone. Without these permissions, Apache will reject the request before it even reaches your application logic, resulting in the generic "Object not found" message.

For more detailed guidance on setting up Laravel environments with XAMPP, refer to the official resources available at [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com).
